words.g: going to be parted from it

1.sense: One long sentence about people fixed in a position. Two groups are named, those of the People of the Book who disbelieved and the idolaters, and the claim is that nothing already in their hands was going to move them off where they stood until the clear proof arrived.

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ told Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that Allah had commanded him to recite this surah to him. Ubayy asked whether Allah had mentioned him by name, and when he was told yes, he wept.
notes.src: Muslim 799, from Anas; also reported by Bukhari

notes.t: Munfakkin is from a verb meaning to come apart, used of a joint coming out of its socket. The image is of people locked into a position who were not going to work themselves loose from it on their own.

This is one of the harder sentences in the Qur'an to construe and the early exegetes said so. The difficulty is what exactly they were not parting from, and whether the arrival of the proof did in fact part them, since the next verses report that many of them did not move.
notes.src: at-Tabari records several constructions of the verse and the later commentators added more

links.why: We do not punish until We have sent a messenger
messengers sent so that nobody would have an argument left against Allah

2.sense: The clear proof of the previous verse turns out to be a person. It is not an argument or a sign in the sky, and the verse identifies him by what he is doing with his mouth rather than by any office he holds.

notes.t: Naming the bayyinah as a man is the point of the pair of verses. A proof that walks into a town, recites, and can be questioned is a different kind of evidence from a miracle that happens once and is over.
Suhuf are loose sheets, not a bound book. The word describes what revelation looked like while it was still coming down in pieces, before anything was gathered between two covers.

Purity is said here of the pages. Another surah says the record is in honoured, raised and purified pages in the hands of noble scribes, so the same description is used of what is written and of who carries it.

links.why: the same pages described as honoured, raised and purified
a messenger raised from among them who recites the verses to them

3.sense: What is on the pages is described in one word, and the word is about posture. The writings stand upright, which in Arabic means they do not lean and nothing in them has to be propped up.

notes.t: Qayyimah is from the root of standing. Applied to a text it means one that holds its own weight, and it is the same word the surah uses two verses later of the religion itself, which ties the book to the practice.
The Qur'an says of itself that it was sent down with no crookedness in it, straight, and puts the word straight in a sentence of its own for emphasis.
Kutub, plural, inside suhuf, plural. Most exegetes read the phrase as the written matters or rulings that the pages carry rather than as separate books stacked inside them.

links.why: the same claim of a book with nothing bent in it
the upright religion named with the same word

4.sense: The people who had a scripture did not divide while they were waiting. They divided after the evidence arrived, which reverses the usual explanation that people disagree because they were not told enough.

notes.t: The order of events is the argument. Division did not come from a shortage of evidence; it came once the evidence was in the room, which means the cause has to be looked for somewhere other than in the information.
The Qur'an makes the same charge about earlier communities more than once, and in one place names the motive plainly as rivalry between themselves rather than any doubt about the message.
Bayyinah is the same word used in verse one, so the proof that was being waited for and the proof they broke apart over are stated to be one and the same thing.

links.why: they divided only after knowledge came, out of rivalry among themselves
the same charge laid against those given the Book

5.sense: After the report of division comes the list they divided over, and it is short. Worship Allah with the thing kept pure for Him, lean away from everything else, stand the prayer, hand over the zakat. The verse then says that this list is the upright religion.

notes.t: Sincerity is not added on top of the command, it is inside it. Mukhlisina lahu-d-din is a state the worshipper is in while worshipping, and jurists cite this verse for the rule that an act done for two audiences is not the act that was asked for.
Hanif is the Qur'an's word for Ibrahim, who is said to have been neither a Jew nor a Christian. Using it here addresses two communities that both traced themselves back to him.
Two of the four items are actions with witnesses, prayer and zakat, and two are conditions of the heart. The verse does not let either half stand alone as the religion.

links.why: I was commanded to worship Allah keeping the religion pure for Him
Ibrahim named hanif and claimed by both groups this surah addresses

6.sense: The two groups named in verse one come back in the same order, and now a verdict is attached to them. The verse states where they are, that they stay there, and then measures them against everything that has been made.

notes.t: The surah is built as a frame. The same two parties open it and close it, and what has changed in between is only that the proof arrived and was answered.
Bariyyah is from a root meaning to originate something out of nothing. Calling them the worst of what was originated measures them against every created thing rather than against other people.
The Qur'an uses this superlative sparingly. In one place the worst of moving creatures are those who will not use their hearing or their reason, which is the same charge in different words.

links.why: the same superlative applied to those who will not believe
what was worshipped beside Allah named alongside its worshippers

7.sense: The opposite verdict in the same frame. Two conditions are given, belief and the deeds that follow it, and the people who hold both are measured against everything made and placed at the top.

notes.t: Two canonical readings stand on the last word, al-bariyyah without a hamza, which is the reading in this Mushaf, and al-bariah with one. The root is the same either way, to bring a thing into being from nothing.
notes.src: the canonical readings differ; Hafs reads al-bariyyah and others read it with the hamza

notes.t: Belief is paired with deeds here as it is throughout the Qur'an. The verse does not call belief on its own the best of creation, and it does not call deeds on their own that either.
The same two conditions are the exception that pulls a life out of loss in Surah al-ʿAsr, where two more are added that require other people to be present.

links.why: the same two conditions used to reverse a verdict on the whole species
a community called the best brought out for people, with its conditions given

8.sense: The reward is described, and then the description is interrupted by something that is not a place. He is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him. The verse then ends by naming the one qualification that all of it depends on.

notes.t: The mutual pleasure appears elsewhere in the Qur'an as the end of the whole matter, and in one place the words that follow it are that this is the great success, said after gardens have already been mentioned.

The condition placed at the end is not a deed. Everything listed is put behind one word, and the word is fear of one's Lord, which is a state a person can be in while walking around and doing nothing visible.

Khashiya is not ordinary fright. The Qur'an uses the same verb when it says that of His servants it is the ones with knowledge who fear Allah, which ties this kind of fear to knowing what is being feared.

links.why: the same mutual pleasure named as the great success
the garden made the home of whoever feared standing before his Lord
